fields.description: Savings plans that bloom as you reach each goal.
fields.intro: Garden is a money app for young Canadians: tell it what you’re saving for, and it builds a plan of small steps and grows flowers and trees as you go. In a team of six at the Sun Life uXperience Design Jam 2024, I designed the app screens and a basic design system.
fields.summary: Designing a savings app that breaks big money goals into small steps and grows a garden as you reach them.
fields.overview: Garden is for young Canadians like Sarah, a busy student saving for her first car. Our team of six designed it in one day at the Sun Life uXperience Design Jam, and we presented it as Sarah’s story in a three-minute live pitch.

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.heading: How might we help young Canadians find, and use the financial tools & education available to them?

children.text: This was Sun Life’s prompt at the uXperience Design Jam, held at the University of Waterloo’s Stratford School on November 2, 2024. Six of us had about six and a half hours to answer it, with a three-minute pitch at the end.

Sun Life’s brief was simple: there are financial tools and education to help young people make money decisions and plan for their goals, but they’re under-used. They asked for something easy and inclusive that helps young Canadians open up about money and feel confident about their financial future.
There were also two workshops that morning: one on financial fluency and one on breaking down barriers with behavioural economics.
We split the work into roles: product, script, slides and two UI designers. I set up the design system and designed the app screens, and the other UI designer made the illustrations.
We told the whole pitch through one person. Sarah is a second-year GBDA student at Waterloo with a long commute to Stratford, so she wants a car, but the $2,000 down payment feels like a mountain.

content.label: Sarah’s week
content.caption: Everything competing for Sarah’s time, from our pitch.

children.text: Between five courses, a part-time job and her friends, money planning keeps getting pushed back. She has never saved this much before and doesn’t know where to start. A chequing account? A high-interest savings account?
Sarah isn’t alone. On our whiteboard, we listed what gets in the way for young people like her, and most of what follows comes back to this list.

content.label: Problems
content.caption: The problems we listed, from the whiteboard.

children.text: Before any screens, there was a whiteboard. Around Sun Life’s question, we listed why young people don’t use financial tools: the time it takes, fear, procrastination and relying on parents. Then came the functions we wanted, visual ideas and the problems above.

content.alt: A whiteboard covered in red marker: Sun Life’s How might we question at the top, then Why not?, Functions, Visual components, a script outline for Sarah, a Growth column (start with a sapling, plant a tree, grow your own forest), Problems, Gamification and Constraints with AI generated advice
content.caption: Our whiteboard from the day.

children.text: The idea we landed on was Garden. It takes one big goal and breaks it into small steps you can act on:
Make a plan
from a goal, in your own words.
Keep track
of your progress as you save.
Find resources
for each step: answers in the app, outside resources and a financial advisor.
Act on the plan
in the app, like saving into a new account.
Garden is its own app, and it points people to Sun Life’s products and advisors along the way.
Why a garden
Progress shows up as a garden: smaller goals grow flowers, and saving and learning grow trees. We built the whole app around it for four reasons:
Progress you can see.
Plants growing feel like progress in a way charts and numbers don’t, and numbers were on our list of problems.
It grows with you.
Saving is slow, like a garden. As Sarah grows, Garden grows with her.
A brand to remember.
The pitch tips we worked from asked for a fun brand with custom illustrations, and a garden gave us one.
Real-world impact.
When your virtual tree is fully grown, a real one gets planted, so the progress means something outside the app.

content.alt: An iPhone showing Garden’s first home screen: Hello, Sarah; Welcome to your Garden with Create a plan, Find resources and Earn badges; and About your Garden, explaining Trees (a real tree is planted after your virtual tree is grown) and Flowers for smaller goals
content.caption: Before the first plan, Home explains how the garden works.

children.text: Anxiety with starting was on our list, and it’s Sarah’s problem too: she doesn’t know which account she needs, let alone how to plan for a car. So planning in Garden starts as a chat. We chose a chat for three reasons:
It’s less intimidating.
Typing a goal in your own words is easier than a form full of money fields.
It’s beginner friendly.
You can start without knowing which account or product you need.
It’s personal.
Garden asks follow-up questions to fit the plan to you.

Sarah types “I need to save $2000 for a car”. Garden asks about her timeline, her income and her saving style, and once she answers, it lays out a Car Savings Plan: $500 every three months, $2,000 over 12 months.

content.alt: Three iPhones with arrows: Create a plan with example goals; Sarah’s message “I need to save $2000 for a car” and Garden asking about Timeline, Your income and Saving style; then the Car Savings Plan with four $500 steps from November 2024 to November 2025, March open with its explanation, and Save and activate plan
content.caption: From a goal to a plan in two messages.

children.text: Each step opens to explain itself, like why it’s $500 every three months, and the Save and activate plan button turns it on.

In our pitch, the first steps are quick on purpose. Drawing on behavioural economics, Garden puts easy steps first to build momentum: Sarah opens a high-interest savings account, links it to Garden and sets up automatic transfers in a few minutes.

Here is where “overwhelmed with numbers” gets its answer. Every plan lives in the Plans tab. Big plans get cards with their total, the next goal and a plant that grows with them. Smaller ones, like a MacBook Pro or a Mexico trip, sit in a list, each with a flower at its own stage.
A toggle at the top switches Plans to Garden, where everything you’ve grown is planted together. Sarah’s garden starts with two flowers and fills in as she finishes goals.

content.alt: Three iPhones with arrows: the Plans tab with cards for Buy Car, Buy House, Retirement Plan and Student Loans, a list of smaller plans (MacBook Pro, Mexico Trip, New Tattoo), each with a flower at its stage, and a New button; the Garden view with two yellow flowers; and the Garden view with a big green tree, a yellow tulip, a sunflower and sprouts
content.caption: Plans, then the garden as it grows.

children.text: Each time Sarah opens Garden, she lands on Home. It leads with a pinned goal, then recent plans with their progress and the badges she has earned, like 500 Saver and 1k Saver.
Earlier versions

Home went through three rougher versions before the final one, and two of them are shown here. Plain progress bars read like the numbers we were trying to get away from, so plans moved to dotted timelines that end in a plant icon showing each plan’s stage. The final home also put the rewards up front, with a flower on the goal card and badges below the plans, and Search got its own tab.

content.alt: Three iPhones with arrows: an early home with a New MacBook Pro card and plain progress bars for Retirement and Student Loan; another early version with Plans as dotted timelines ending in plant icons and an Ask button; and the final home with a sunflower on the goal card, Recent Plans, earned badges and a Search tab
content.caption: Two earlier versions of Home, then the final one.

children.text: Two more problems on our list were “afraid to reach out” and “intimidating to younger users”. Next to the first, our whiteboard says “make it less human”. In Garden, help sits inside the app: Sarah can learn from Resources and ask Search questions on her own.
Resources holds knowledge cards on topics like OSAP loans, GICs, savings and buying a car, each with its own minigames. A list below covers leasing a house, mutual funds and retirement.

Search takes questions in plain words, like “How do I open a savings account?” Its answers come from Garden’s resource bank, and a note under the questions says Search doesn’t generate new data or store yours.

content.alt: Two iPhones: Resources with Search Knowledge Cards, cards for OSAP Loans, What is a GIC?, Savings and Buying a Car with their minigame counts, and a list of Leasing a house, Mutual Funds and Retirement; and Search with How can we help?, three suggested questions and a note that Garden Search answers from a resource bank

children.text: Nudges
Garden also reaches Sarah outside the app. In our pitch, two years after her car, a widget on her home screen asks if she’s considered an emergency fund.

content.alt: Two iPhones with an arrow: a phone home screen with a Garden widget asking “Have you considered an emergency fund?”, then Garden’s home with the same suggestion in a green card at the top
content.caption: The widget, then the same nudge on Home.

children.text: On Home, the same suggestion sits at the top, based on her journey so far. A lock-screen notification can do the same: “Pssst... have you considered an emergency fund?”
Every screen in this story is built on the basic design system I set up. Each choice had its own reason:
Green for growth.
Garden green ties the app to plants, growth and money.
Sunflower yellow for Sun Life.
It nods to Sun Life’s slogan, “Life’s brighter under the sun”.
Warm type.
Hedvig Letters Serif headings, with Inter for everything else and soft colours around them, keep Garden friendly and calm, not like a bank.

content.alt: Garden’s design system on one panel: colour swatches for Garden green #399C74, Mint #C2E0D4, Sunflower #EDBC33, Forest #184231 and Warm grey #64615B; type samples, “Hello, Sarah” in Hedvig Letters Serif and “New MacBook Pro” in Inter; and three components from the app: the New MacBook Pro goal card, the plan list with dotted timelines and plant icons, and the Home, Plans, Resources and Search tab bar
content.caption: Colours, type and components from the final screens.

children.text: We presented Garden in a three-minute live pitch, told as Sarah’s story. It followed her from a $2,000 down payment that felt like a mountain to reaching her goal, then two years on to an emergency fund. Alongside the pitch, we made a clickable prototype of the app.
What I learned
Pitch it as a story.
Following Sarah made the features make sense in three minutes.
Make progress visible.
Flowers and trees make saving feel like progress, not just numbers.
Summary

Garden started with Sun Life’s question and one overwhelmed student. For the anxiety of starting, it plans by chat and puts quick steps first. For the numbers, it grows a garden. For finding and using the tools, it gives each step its own resources and a way to act on it in the app. In one day, our team of six turned that into a clickable prototype and a three-minute story.
